title: Region-Conscious Resource Contracts & CRUD API Primer
content:
Purpose and scope:
This note captures a compact, practical set of conventions for the control-plane data model and CRUD API behaviors when resources are region-aware and routed across clusters. Focus: resource identity and tenancy, environment semantics, region/cluster binding, routing policy surface, and API-level guarantees (idempotency / consistency / soft-delete / versioning).

Why this matters:
- Routing and failover need a single source of truth for where a resource is ‘owned’ and where it can be served from.
- Misaligned IDs/namespaces across regions produce subtle routing and caching bugs.
- APIs should make intended binding explicit to avoid implicit, brittle routing heuristics in callers.

High-level model (phrasing intentionally operational):
- Resource: an application-level object that can be served by inference nodes (examples: model-deployment, routing-rule, dataset-mount).
- Environment: logical stage (dev, staging, prod) that constrains lifecycle policies and allowed operations.
- Region: cloud region string (e.g., us-west-2) where clusters exist.
- Cluster: a deployment unit inside a region that hosts compute and local storage. Clusters have capacity, labels (gpu-type, zone), and an optional affinity tag.
- Binding: a first-class attribute that ties a Resource -> (Environment, Region, Cluster-scope). Binding is declarative: it answers the question ‘where is this resource valid/owned?’

Core data fields for a Resource record (minimal, normalized):
- id (string): globally unique, opaque (uuid-like).
- name (string): human-friendly name, unique per environment and owner namespace.
- owner_id (string): team or tenant id.
- env (string): one of dev|staging|prod.
- allowed_regions (list of strings): regions the resource is allowed to be scheduled to.
- primary_region (string): the canonical region for ownership and data locality (may be null for global resources).
- cluster_selector (string|map): optional selector expression used by scheduler to pick cluster (gpu:ampere, disk:ssd, etc.). Represented as a short expression string to keep schema flat in Drive docs.
- routing_policy (string): shorthand pointer to routing behavior (e.g., prefer-primary, geo-failover, latency-based, cost-prefer).
- status (string): active|deleting|deleted|failed|provisioning.
- version (string): resource schema version / incremented on mutating updates (use RFC-like semver or a monotonic token).
- annotations (string): freeform notes / links (single string with newline-separated key:val pairs).

Naming and identity rules (operational):
- id is allocated by control plane; clients should never derive ids from names.
- name uniqueness is scoped to (owner_id, env). This prevents cross-team collisions while keeping names readable.
- canonical references in URLs use id; name-based endpoints are convenience only and can return a redirect with id.

Region/cluster binding semantics:
- primary_region indicates authoritative location for data and owner-level metadata. For read-heavy metadata, control plane queries should hit primary_region first for lowest staleness.
- allowed_regions is a superset of regions where the scheduler may place instances; routing_policy + cluster_selector influence the runtime decision.
- cluster_binding objects are ephemeral artifacts produced by the scheduler: ResourceBinding {resource_id, cluster_id, region, started_at, lifecycle_state}. These live in the runtime plane, not as first-class persistent resource properties (keeps resource record small).

API contract surface (summary):
- Base path: /api/v1/platform/resources
- Use JSON over TLS. All write operations require an If-Match: <version> header for optimistic concurrency.

Create resource (POST /api/v1/platform/resources)
- Body: { name, owner_id, env, primary_region?, allowed_regions?, cluster_selector?, routing_policy? }
- Response: 201 Created { id, version, location: /api/v1/platform/resources/{id} }
- Behavior: server assigns id and version. If name already exists in (owner_id, env) return 409.
- Idempotency: client-supplied Idempotency-Key header accepted; server returns same resource for repeated requests with same key for up to 24h.

Read resource (GET /api/v1/platform/resources/{id})
- Query params: region_hint (optional), include_bindings (bool, default false)
- Behavior: reads are served from a regional replica. If region_hint is provided, prefer local replica; otherwise route to primary_region for authoritative view.
- Staleness: eventual across regions; response includes a metadata header X-Resource-Version and X-Source-Region.

Update resource (PATCH /api/v1/platform/resources/{id})
- Body: patch-style (JSON Merge Patch).
- Must include If-Match header with current version. Server validates primary_region changes (see constraints).
- Allowed changes: routing_policy, allowed_regions (add/remove), cluster_selector, annotations.
- Primary_region change: elevated workflow — PATCH can set primary_region but result = pending_migration until background job finishes data move; status flips to provisioning.
- Response: 200 with new version token.

Delete resource (DELETE /api/v1/platform/resources/{id})
- Behavior: soft-delete by default. Moves status -> deleting and records tombstone with deleted_at. Soft-delete window default 30d (configurable per owner/contract).
- Hard delete: admin-only operation, idempotent.

Idempotency and concurrency patterns:
- All mutating endpoints require If-Match for optimistic control. This avoids lost-update problems with cross-region eventual consistency.
- Create supports Idempotency-Key to de-duplicate retries.
- Version tokens are opaque strings; clients must treat them as integers/strings and not attempt to infer ordering except via server-provided headers.

Routing policy surface (exposed on resource record):
- prefer-primary: always route to primary if available. Fallback to allowed_regions by proximity/cost.
- geo-failover: prefer replicas in region of request; failover order determined by allowed_regions list.
- latency-based: scheduler uses measured p50/p95 to choose cluster. Requires observability wiring.
- cost-prefer: choose cheaper clusters first (useful for non-latency-sensitive workloads).
- sticky-session: for stateful resources, prefer previously-affined cluster unless unavailable.

Validation and governance rules (examples):
- allowed_regions must be subset of company-supported regions for the owner tier. Attempts to add unsupported regions return 400 with reason.
- primary_region may not be removed from allowed_regions.
- env transitions: prod -> staging is disallowed; upgrades must follow explicit migration plan.

Operational notes and patterns:
- Keep resource records small: move high-volume runtime data to runtime plane (bindings, health checks). Control plane holds authoritative config and policy.
- Provide a region-aware cache layer in the control plane API edge that emits X-Stale-After and X-Source-Region headers to help clients reason about freshness.
- Implement a migration controller for primary_region change: it orchestrates cross-region snapshots, data transfer, and atomic cutover of the resource version.

Edge cases / open questions (placeholders to drive follow-ups):
- Global resources (no primary_region): how to reconcile write conflicts when multiple regions accept writes? Suggestion: forbid mutating operations unless request includes a write-intent header pointing to a single region controller.
- Cross-owner lookups: admin APIs only; beware of name collisions in aggregated views.
- Soft-delete retention tuning: default 30d may be too long for high-cardinality resources; consider per-owner quotas.

Migration checklist example when changing primary_region:
1) Validate destination region capacity and owner quotas.
2) Snapshot resource-backed data (if any) and copy to destination region storage.
3) Drain new provisioned instances in destination region to warm caches.
4) Flip primary_region in control plane with a new version token and set status -> provisioning.
5) Wait for scheduler to bind new cluster instances.
6) Cut live traffic to new region and mark old bindings for graceful shutdown.
7) Confirm data integrity and mark status -> active.

Suggested next steps / TODOs:
- Draft API OpenAPI spec for the surface above (include headers, error codes, sample payloads).
- Wire X-Source-Region in the API gateway and surface in SDKs.
- Implement a small simulator to exercise primary_region change flows under network partitions.
- Add a Confluence page with migration runbook and roles (owner, infra, data-migration).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally concise rather than exhaustive. I prefer concrete rules that avoid magic routing heuristics in clients.
- Comments welcome on routing_policy design — especially on how many policy knobs we should expose vs. server-side heuristics.

References and links:
- See linked artifacts (JIRA, PR) for early drafts and scheduler integration notes.
- Related: region-aware service registry discussions in eng slack (#region-routing)

End of note.
